title: How Psychopaths Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain psychopathy: how it differs from sociopathy and psychosis, its history from Philippe Pinel and J.L.A. Cox to the coining of the term, Hervey Cleckley's work and Robert Hare's two-factor model and Psychopathy Checklist, prevalence and demographics (gender, age, race claims and criticism), the brain research on the amygdala and prefrontal cortex, treatment options such as decompression therapy, and advice on dealing with psychopaths. The episode closes with a plug for John Ronson's book The Psychopath Test, Chuck's new podcast Movie Crush, and listener mail about the Stuff You Should Know Army.
topics: factor one and factor two psychopathy

entities.name: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM)

segments.title: Opening banter and psychopathy overview
segments.summary: The hosts introduce psychopathy, note misconceptions, say many leaders may show some psychopathic traits, and explain the spectrum and threshold idea. They estimate about one percent of the population are psychopaths and discuss high-functioning psychopaths in white-collar jobs.

segments.title: History of the term psychopathy
segments.summary: The hosts trace historical and cross-cultural references to psychopath-like figures, from Theophrastus and Aristotle to the Bible, and mention names used in other cultures. They describe Philippe Pinel's early descriptions, the later labels like moral insanity, and J.L.A. Cox's coining of the term psychopathy.

segments.title: Psychopathy versus sociopathy and psychosis
segments.summary: The hosts explain why sociopathy was used for much of the twentieth century, citing a nurture-based view and confusion with psychosis. They distinguish psychosis, a loss of grip on reality, from psychopathy, a moral condition in which reality testing is intact. The DSM later replaced sociopathy with antisocial personality disorder.

segments.title: Hervey Cleckley, Robert Hare, and the two factors
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Hervey Cleckley's book The Mask of Sanity and Robert Hare's Psychopathy Checklist. They describe factor one (interpersonal and affective traits such as lack of remorse) and factor two (behavioral traits such as impulsivity), and say the DSM focuses on factor two, while the checklist captures factor one.
topics: factor one and factor two psychopathy

segments.title: Demographics: age, children, race and gender
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the difficulty of studying psychopaths, since most data come from prison populations and self-reporting is rare. They cover possible decline with age, the controversy over diagnosing children, Richard Lynn's racially charged claims and their criticism, and the finding that men are more often psychopaths along with the idea that female psychopathy may present differently.

segments.title: The Psychopathy Checklist (PCL-R) scoring
segments.summary: The hosts walk through the twenty items of the Psychopathy Checklist, each scored 0 to 2, and note that a score of about 30 out of 40 (varying by country, often 26 to 30) indicates psychopathy. They explain that the test takes hours, requires a trained psychologist, and that high-functioning psychopaths may score differently from those who fail in life.

segments.title: Dealing with psychopaths
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how psychopaths may research interviewers in advance, citing Hannibal Lecter as an example. They describe the common advice to keep distance and not give psychopaths what they want, and Chuck suggests future generations may see current treatment as harsh, since psychopaths may be physically different in the brain.

segments.title: Brain research: amygdala, prefrontal cortex, genetics, and treatment
segments.summary: The hosts review brain imaging studies showing differences in the amygdala and the prefrontal cortex, the role of emotion in socialization, and twin studies suggesting genetic contributions. They discuss treatment, saying there is no cure, group therapy may make psychopaths worse, and decompression treatment that rewards good behavior is being tried with kids.

segments.title: The Psychopath Test book and Movie Crush
segments.summary: The hosts recommend John Ronson's book The Psychopath Test and mention his appearance on a live show. Chuck promotes his new podcast Movie Crush, where he talks with guests about their favorite movie, and says John Ronson's pick was Let the Right One In.

segments.title: Listener mail: Stuff You Should Know Army
segments.summary: A listener named Tony from Sacramento writes about meeting Stuff You Should Know Army members in real life. The hosts describe the community's Facebook group and social media accounts.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners, point to social media and email contacts, and sign off.
